deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a fair copy, apparently in the hand of the editor (H. Weber), of item XXVI 'Beispiele von Flächen kleinsten Inhalts bei gegebener Begrenzung' for Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (1876). The page numbers S.296/298 refer to Riemann's paper 'Über die Fläche vom kleinsten Inhalt bei gegebener Begrenzung' as printed in the Werke. The footnote says Example I comes from a single sheet in Riemann's Nachlass, where the result is stated briefly but completely. For Example II Riemann left only a remark that a solution is possible, so the editor is responsible for working it out. The footnote also cites Schwarz's 1871 Berlin monograph.

Problem I (setup). Three straight lines L1, L2, L3 are given. L1 meets L2 in a corner A, and L2 meets L3 in a corner B. L1 and L3 are skew, with shortest distance C. Find the minimal surface spanned by them: a surface with two corners and one strip running to infinity between L1 and L3. The angles between the lines are απ, βπ, γπ.

Gauss map. Along a straight boundary line the normal stays perpendicular to that line, so each boundary line maps onto an arc of a great circle. The image of the surface is therefore a spherical triangle with angles απ, βπ, γπ. Its positive area (α+β+γ−1)π forces α+β+γ>1.

Parametrisation. The surface is mapped conformally onto the half-plane of a complex variable t. The real points a, b, c correspond to the two corners and to the infinite strip (Riemann, Art. 13).

The function u. Riemann's auxiliary function u (whose real part gives the coordinate along a distinguished direction) has a logarithmic singularity only at the strip. So:
- du = const · dt / ((t−c)·sqrt((t−a)(t−b))).
- Integrating: u = const · log[(p−q)/(p+q)], with p = sqrt((t−a)/(c−a)) and q = sqrt((t−b)/(c−b)).
- (My check) d/dt log((p−q)/(p+q)) = sqrt((c−a)(c−b)) / ((t−c)·sqrt((t−a)(t−b))), so the formula is exact up to the constant.

Normalisation a=0, b=∞, c=1 (allowed by a Möbius map of the half-plane):
- du = const · dt/((1−t)·sqrt t).
- u = const · log((1−sqrt t)/(1+sqrt t)).

The constant. It equals i·C/(2π), with C the shortest distance between the two skew lines. (My filling, not on the page:) Passing round t=1 in the half-plane, the logarithm jumps by ±iπ, so u jumps by ∓C/2. Riemann's coordinate is u plus its conjugate, i.e. 2·Re(u), so it jumps by C. This is the separation of L1 and L3 measured along their common perpendicular. That perpendicular is the normal direction at the infinite end of the strip, i.e. the triangle vertex of angle γπ, placed at η=0 or ∞.

The functions k1, k2. Following Art. 14 (S.298), put k1 = sqrt(du/dη) and k2 = η·sqrt(du/dη). Here η is the stereographic image of the normal, so η = k2/k1. These are finite and single-valued in the t-plane except at 0, ∞, 1.

Local analysis (continued on the next page) identifies k1, k2 as two branches of the Riemann P-function
P( 1/4−α/2, 1/4−β/2, −γ/2 ; 1/4+α/2, 1/4+β/2, γ/2 ; t ).
- The exponent differences α, β, γ match the triangle angles.
- The exponent sum is 1, as Riemann's P-function requires.
- η is the quotient of two branches.

The page thus reduces the Plateau problem for this skew-line contour to hypergeometric functions, via the Gauss map and Riemann's P-function.
errors: No mathematical errors found. The general integral is correct, with the constant sqrt((c−a)(c−b)) absorbed into 'const'.
Sign/branch: the general formula with b→∞ gives log((sqrt t − 1)/(sqrt t + 1)). This differs from log((1−sqrt t)/(1+sqrt t)) by the additive constant iπ, which is harmless.

The value const = i·C/(2π) is stated without proof. Whether the jump of u is C/2 or C depends on Riemann's normalisation (u versus 2·Re u). I could not check this beyond plausibility; it is consistent if the coordinate is u + ū.

results.what: Closed-form integral of dt/((t−c)·sqrt((t−a)(t−b))) as a logarithm
results.modern_name: elementary integral (third-kind integral on a genus-0 curve)

results.what: Minimal surface bounded by two intersecting-line corners and a strip between two skew lines: Gauss image is a spherical triangle, and the Weierstrass-type data k1, k2 are branches of a Riemann P-function with exponents (1/4 ± α/2, 1/4 ± β/2, ± γ/2)
results.modern_name: Riemann–Schwarz solution of Plateau's problem for polygonal contours via the Gauss map and hypergeometric (Schwarz triangle) functions
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (Nachlass, published in Werke 1876, XXVI, ed. Weber); related work by Schwarz 1865–1871

results.what: The constant in u is fixed by the distance C between the skew lines through the logarithmic singularity at the strip
results.modern_name: period / flux condition at an end of a minimal surface

deep.surprise_reason: This is the editor's fair copy of Example XXVI, printed in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (1876); the footnote itself says Example I is from Riemann's Nachlass. The content is published and attributed to Riemann. The method is that of his published minimal-surface paper, applied to a specific contour.

checkable.sympy: a,b,c,t=symbols('a b c t'); p=sqrt((t-a)/(c-a)); q=sqrt((t-b)/(c-b)); simplify(diff(log((p-q)/(p+q)),t) - sqrt((c-a)*(c-b))/((t-c)*sqrt((t-a)*(t-b))))  # ==0 (test numerically, e.g. a=0,b=2,c=-1,t=3)
checkable.asserts: The general log formula is an antiderivative of const/((t−c)·sqrt((t−a)(t−b))).
d/dt log((1−√t)/(1+√t)) = −1/((1−t)√t), i.e. the special case a=0, b=∞, c=1 holds up to the sign of the constant.
The six P-function exponents sum to 1 (Riemann's condition).
A ±iπ jump of the logarithm round t=1 gives a jump of ∓C/2 in u, hence C in u + ū.

transcription_corrections: 'Die erste dieser Beispiele' should most likely read 'Das erste dieser Beispiele'.

The final citation '(Fortsetzung einer speciellen Minimalfläche Berlin 1871.)' is most likely '(Bestimmung einer speciellen Minimalfläche, Berlin 1871)', Schwarz's prize memoir; the previous page cites this same title.
The struck-out phrase in the footnote is the Monatsberichte der Berliner Akademie 1872 reference, deleted in favour of the 1871 monograph.
The bracketed '(Note unter den Text)' is an editorial instruction to set the footnote at the foot of the page, not part of the mathematical text.
